title: Verifier-Guided Prompting for Intent-to-Configuration Translation: A Preregistered NetOps Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory trial to measure whether constrained prompting plus a deterministic generate→verify→repair loop improves deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness when translating operator natural-language intents into low-level device configurations. Design: N=150 synthetic intents sampled from a deterministic generator, shared_initial_candidate execution semantics, model = gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, one initial generation per intent shared across baseline and guarded conditions, guarded pipeline permitted at most one repair call. Results (artifact-grounded): baseline = 149/150 (99.333%); guarded = 150/150 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.006667 (≈0.67 percentage points); exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Provider accounting: completed episodes = 300; model_calls_used = 151; repair-stage invocations = 1. Interpretation: under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and a one-repair budget the guarded workflow yielded a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement over an already near-ceiling baseline; we identify a ceiling-effect threat to preregistered power planning and provide methodological prescriptions to avoid it. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived in the supplied execution bundle referenced by the execution manifest.

sections.introduction:
Natural-language intent interfaces lower operator burden by letting humans express desired network changes as free text that is automatically translated into executable device configurations. Prior work shows single-pass LLM outputs commonly exhibit syntactic errors, omissions, or semantic violations that can produce unsafe or availability-reducing states if applied directly [1][2][3]. A standard defensive pattern is a generate→verify→repair architecture: an LLM produces a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks task-level invariants, and a repair or human gate corrects violations before execution [4][5]. Security analyses further motivate deterministic gating because unguarded multi-tool agents can convert false textual claims into harmful actions [6].

Research question. After a fresh literature review we preregistered study_cand_2026_b2_v1 to test a confined confirmatory question: does constrained prompting (structured templates with explicit semantic slots) combined with deterministic verifier-guided iterative feedback materially increase deterministic-verifier semantic-correctness of NL→configuration translation versus an unconstrained baseline under a paired design? The preregistration and analysis plan were frozen prior to observing any model outputs.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifactized paired confirmatory trial measuring deterministic-verifier pass/fail on a programmatically generated synthetic corpus (N=150 paired intents). (2) Artifact-backed numeric outcomes showing that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics and a one-repair budget, the guarded pipeline raised verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (+0.67 pp), a numerically negligible and statistically non-significant improvement (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). (3) A methodological recommendation: preregistered NetOps trials should include baseline-calibration pilots and explicitly state generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate vs independent sampling) because these choices materially change the estimand and interpretability of repair-stage benefits.
sections.related_work: Related literature covers intent-translation evaluations, verifier-guided repair systems, formal verifier tooling, and agentic/tool-augmented safety analyses. Evaluations of NL→configuration pipelines document that free-text prompts often produce omissions or incorrect sequencing that violate required invariants, producing modest semantic-correctness rates on heterogeneous task banks [1]. Systems that integrate deterministic verification into generation workflows (generate→verify→repair and verifier-guided fine-tuning) report improved practical correctness, but effect sizes depend on baseline competence, verifier expressiveness, repair budget, and sampling semantics [2][3]. Formal network-verification tools (e.g., NetKAT-family verifiers, symbolic reachability engines) provide deterministic oracles for many invariants and are suitable as gating layers, but their protocol coverage, scale limits, and abstraction gaps can introduce measurement or coverage bias [5]. Security analyses demonstrate claim-to-action and prompt-injection risks in multi-tool LLM agents and motivate auditable verifier verdicts and conservative gating [4]. Our trial differs from many prior evaluations by preregistering a paired confirmatory design, enforcing shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded contrasts use the same sampled candidate per intent, constraining the repair budget to ≤1, and using a deterministic verifier as the binary oracle—choices that intentionally bound the observable marginal effect of a guarded repair under the chosen estimand.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered as study_cand_2026_b2_v1 and frozen before any model outputs. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline evaluated with an exact two-sided McNemar test on deterministic-verifier pass/fail outcomes. Confirmatory sample: N=150 distinct synthetic intents from a deterministic generator stratified across four intent families. The preregistration specified inclusion/exclusion rules (rule-based ambiguity detector, parser/verifier-coverage checks), a retry policy (one retry on provider timeouts), and a power target to detect an absolute +15 percentage-point improvement with ≈80% power under conservative discordant-pair assumptions.

Execution semantics and mapping from preregistration to the executed contrast. Crucially, the archived execution adapter enforced shared_initial_candidate semantics: for every intent exactly one initial model generation was produced and that identical sampled candidate was used to evaluate both the baseline and guarded conditions. The guarded pipeline was permitted at most one additional repair call only if the deterministic verifier failed the initial candidate. As a result, the actual confirmatory contrast tested and archived is guarded (C) versus baseline (A) under shared_initial_candidate semantics; the preregistered conceptual three-condition design (A: baseline, B: constrained, C: guarded) mapped to an executed paired comparison where B (constrained-only as an independent first-pass condition) was not run as an independent first-pass draw across conditions under this adapter policy. Therefore, secondary confirmatory contrasts that would require independent first-pass samples (B vs A or C vs B under independent-per-condition sampling) were not executed and are not supported by the archived paired artifacts. This mapping was preregistered conceptually but the execution contract (shared_initial_candidate, one initial generation per task) determines the precise estimand realized in the archived run; we report that estimand and its artifact-grounded results.

Model, sampling, and deterministic validator. Declared model: gpt-5-mini (provider record: openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" and temperature = null (unset); because no numeric temperature or fixed random seed was enforced, independent API sessions may produce nondeterministic outputs. Deterministic verifier: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version = 5.0) applied a full_intent_constraint_validation rule and returned boolean pass/fail verdicts and per-episode diagnostics used as the binary endpoint.

Task generator, prechecks, and scoring. Confirmatory tasks came from deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 (topologies limited to 4–32 nodes). Parser-to-verifier mapping unit-tests were run before batch evaluation and passed; the preregistered exclusion rules (ambiguous intents or unsupported verifier features) were applied deterministically prior to model calls—no confirmatory exclusions occurred in the archived run. Scoring used the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 full_intent_constraint_validation rule; each episode produced normalized_configuration text that was compared to the preregistered reference invariants for pass/fail determination.

Analysis plan and preregistered procedures. Primary analysis used an exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired contingency counts (n_11, n_10, n_01, n_00) and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed = 1729). The preregistered missingness policy excluded incomplete pairs from the primary test (complete_pair_primary). Secondary contrasts and multiplicity corrections were preregistered but, given the execution semantics noted above, they were not realized as independent-condition comparisons in the archived artifacts. All analysis code and artifacts are archived and referenced in the execution manifest.
sections.results:
Execution and provider accounting. The archived run completed as planned: completed_episode_count = 300 and complete_pair_count = 150. Provider accounting: model_calls_used = 151; completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 151; failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 0; stage_counts recorded shared_initial_generation = 150 and repair = 1. Contamination checks and mapping unit-tests passed; contamination_summary.csv is empty.

Primary numerical outcomes. The paired contingency (guarded × baseline) from analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv: n_11 = 149, n_10 = 1, n_01 = 0, n_00 = 0. Per-condition success rates: baseline_success_rate = 149/150 = 0.9933333333333333; guarded_success_rate = 150/150 = 1.0. Paired absolute difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00666666666666671 (≈0.67 percentage points). Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.02] (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729). These values are reported verbatim from the archived analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv).

Repair diagnostics and iterations. Only one guarded repair invocation occurred (1/150) and it converted a single initially failing candidate to a verifier pass. Median revision iterations for guarded episodes = 0 (IQR = 0). Representative validator traces (validation_before, validation_after, normalized_configuration, violation_codes) for several tasks are archived and document the verifier behavior and difficulty markers.

Power assumptions and inferential consequence. The preregistered power calculation assumed a much lower baseline success rate and targeted detection of a +15 percentage-point absolute improvement with ≈80% power. The observed baseline_success_rate ≈ 99.33% produced a ceiling effect that invalidated those preregistered power assumptions: with n_11 = 149 and only a single discordant pair there is virtually no discordant-pair information to detect the planned effect size. No post-preregistration analytic changes were made; the reported exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI follow the preregistered paired_binary_analysis_v1 procedure applied to the realized paired data.

Representative example. Task-000001 (intent: migrate edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600 with safe shutdown/restore) returned the same shared-initial candidate across conditions; normalized_configuration matched the preregistered reference, parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, and valid = true. Stored responses and validator traces for representative tasks (000001–000006) are archived in the execution bundle.
sections.discussion:
Ceiling effect and methodological lesson. The principal scientific lesson is methodological: preregistered NetOps trials require a baseline-calibration pilot to estimate baseline competence and discordant-pair rates before committing to final N or task difficulty. When generators produce tightly specified intents with constrained allowed action spaces and a verifier that matches those invariants, a capable LLM can produce near-ceiling single-shot correctness, leaving no headroom for repair-stage benefits under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Sampling semantics, estimand interpretation, and operational trade-offs. The shared_initial_candidate enforcement makes the guarded−baseline contrast a pure marginal-repair estimand: it isolates the effect of applying at most one repair to a fixed initial candidate. Alternative semantics—independent per-condition sampling, multiple initial draws, or larger repair budgets—answer different operational questions (expected pass-rate under independent deployment sampling, cost–benefit of re-sampling, diminishing returns of additional repairs) and generally require more model calls and different power calculations. Practitioners should select sampling semantics and repair budgets aligned with deployment constraints and incorporate model-call accounting into power and cost planning. Our archived provider accounting (model_calls_used = 151; repair invocations = 1) quantifies the guarded design cost under the one-repair budget.

Operational value beyond pass/fail. Deterministic guarded workflows yield auditable artifacts (normalized configurations, violation codes, parsed_command_count) that aid triage and human review even when marginal pass-rate gains are small. These observability improvements can reduce human triage time and provide explicit diagnostics to drive targeted automated repairs, benefits not captured by a single binary endpoint.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: adapter-enforced call budgets and pre-execution mapping unit-tests mitigated cross-condition leakage; all deterministic consistency checks passed in the archived reconciliation. Construct validity: the deterministic verifier pass/fail is a proxy for semantic correctness and depends on mapping code and verifier coverage; any uncovered verifier-coverage gap would bias measurement. External validity: experiments used a single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic tasks on small topologies (4–32 nodes); results do not generalize to other models, larger topologies, or vendor-specific CLI idiosyncrasies. Security: the trial did not assess adversarial prompt-injection; separate adversarial evaluations are required to characterize claim-to-action risks. Conclusion validity: the preregistered detectable-effect target was not met due to the observed ceiling, underscoring the need for pilot calibration.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory trial that, under shared_initial_candidate semantics and a one-repair budget, compared baseline free-text prompting with constrained-template prompting plus deterministic verifier-guided repair. On a deterministic synthetic corpus with gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 the guarded pipeline increased verifier pass rate from 149/150 to 150/150 (≈0.67 pp), a numerically small and statistically non-significant difference (exact McNemar p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.02]). The main contribution is methodological: preregistered NetOps experiments must include baseline-calibration pilots and explicitly declare generation semantics and repair budgets so that estimands match deployment constraints and power planning is preserved. Artifact bundles, code, seeds, and verifier traces are archived to enable reproducible follow-up experiments that vary sampling semantics, repair budgets, model diversity, and topology scale.

limitations: Single-model constraint: experiments used only gpt-5-mini; results do not generalize across other models or sizes.

Synthetic corpus and scale: tasks were programmatically generated and limited to verifier-capable small topologies (4–32 nodes); external validity to production WANs and heterogeneous vendor CLIs is untested.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and execution contract limited repair budget to at most one guarded repair call per intent; different generation semantics or larger repair budgets may yield different outcomes.

Ceiling effect and preregistration mismatch: baseline correctness was far higher than the pilot assumptions used for power calculations (planned detectable effect = 15 percentage points), reducing the trial's ability to demonstrate benefit and illustrating sensitivity to baseline calibration.

Verifier coverage and specification translation: the study measures deterministic verifier pass/fail on the preregistered invariants but does not claim safety guarantees beyond the deterministic validator's modeled properties.

Security and adversarial robustness: the experiment did not evaluate adversarial prompt-injection or adversary-driven intents; separate targeted studies are required to assess claim-to-action vulnerabilities in agentic NetOps workflows.
